# What Software Owes You or, Douglas’s Oath To This Work

*A candidate for the Legacy AI / Floyd's Labs Standards & Practices collection.
Offered as prose, not law. It earns its place only if we make it truth.
---

## Who this software or application we build is for

Everyone. Because everyone is a beginner somewhere.

The engineer who has run servers for thirty years picks up a phone app for the
first time and is a beginner. A child opens a homework tool and is a beginner.
A tired parent, at the end of a long day, opens anything at all — beginner.

Most software is built for people who already know the software. That is a
strange way to build things, and it leaves out almost everyone at the exact
moment they arrive.

This document describes what a software platform owes the people who use it,
if its goal is to welcome every level of user — the child, the elder, the
expert, the exhausted, the one who simply does not have time to learn its
ways.

It is written in plain words on purpose. If a sentence here needs a
dictionary, that sentence is wrong.

---

## The promises software owes you

### 1. You never need to know what you were never taught

Software may not assume you arrived knowing it. Whatever it needs from you,
it teaches you at the moment it needs it — in one short sentence, right there,
not in a manual somewhere else.

### 2. It always tells you what happened

After anything happens — success, failure, or nothing — the software says so,
in plain words you can repeat to another person. No codes. No silence. No
"Done." with no explanation of what was done.

### 3. It tells you what you can do next

Every screen and every message is a map, not a dead end. The software names
your choices out loud: *you can do this, or this.* You should never have to
guess what is possible. You cannot be expected to want what you were never
shown.

### 4. It tells you what only you can do

Some decisions belong to a person and cannot be made for them — what gets
published, what gets deleted, what gets paid for. Good software says so,
plainly, at the exact moment the decision becomes yours. It never lets you
discover afterwards that you were responsible for something you were never
told about.

### 5. It tells you what happens without you

Some things continue on their own — a watch, a timer, a helper working in the
background. The software says what is still running, so you can walk away with
a clear head, and it tells you what came of it when you return.

### 6. When it fails, it teaches

An error that only says something went wrong is half an error. Software that
fails must say three things: what went wrong, how to fix it, and what you can
do right now. A failure you can learn from is worth more than a success you
cannot understand.

### 7. It never shames you for not knowing

There is no "obviously," no "as you know," no punishment for curiosity, no
door that locks because you opened it in the wrong order. Not knowing is the
normal condition of every person, in every new place, forever. Software that
forgets this is software that works for almost no one.

### 8. One door, for everyone

The expert and the first-timer walk through the same door. The simple way is
the real way — not a toy copy of the real way. Depth is always available, on
request, but it is never a toll charged at the entrance.

### 9. It carries what you would have to remember

Where you were, what you chose, what is still waiting — the software keeps
these, so you can put them down. Your attention is the rarest thing you own,
and software should spend it like the treasure it is.

### 10. It waits for you

You may leave. You may come back tomorrow, or next month. The work is where
you left it, nothing was lost, and the software picks up the thread with you
as if you had never gone.

### 11. It proves what it claims

If it says a job succeeded, you can see the result. If it says a file is
safe, you can open it. Trust is earned by showing, not by asserting. And when
the software does not know something, it says "I don't know" — in those words.

### 12. It never lies about you

It does not say you approved what you did not approve, decided what you did
not decide, or wrote what you did not write. When software speaks about you,
it speaks the truth about you, or it says nothing.

### 13. If you cannot see, hear, type, or read well — it still welcomes you

Not as a special mode bolted on at the end, but as a guest expected from the
first day. A tool that only works for the strong is a tool that fails the
rest of us, and the rest of us is everyone, eventually.

---

## The one idea underneath all of it

**The user is intelligent and busy.** Not ignorant and lazy. Intelligent —
capable of anything they are shown. Busy — unable to spare what you waste.

Software built on that belief tears down the wall between the people who make
technology and the people who need it. Children, elders, experts, and
strangers walk in the same door, because the door was built human-sized.

---

## A note on what this document is

This is not a law and it does not call itself one. Documents do not become
true by describing themselves as binding; they become true when people find
them so. If these promises turn out to be real — if the software that keeps
them earns back time and trust — then it will have earned whatever place it
is given.
